scenes.text: Polar bears aren't actually white. Their skin underneath is black.
And their fur isn't white either.
Each hair has no pigment at all. It's see-through, with a hollow core.
So why do they look white? The clear hairs scatter and reflect sunlight.
It's the same trick that makes snow and ice look white.
Scientists once wondered if the hairs piped sunlight down to the skin, like fiber optic cables.
But when researchers tested that idea, the fur absorbed most of the ultraviolet light instead.
Their coat has two layers: long guard hairs on top, and a dense, short underfur below.
Under the skin there's a layer of fat up to about four inches thick.
All that insulation works so well that polar bears have more trouble overheating than getting cold.
Big males can weigh up to thirteen hundred pounds, and they overheat quickly when they run.
Their fur can even change color.
Oils from the seals they eat can turn it yellow.
And in some zoos, algae from their pools grew inside the hollow hairs and turned bears green.
Did you know polar bears had black skin? Tell me below.

title: Polar bears aren't white. Their skin is black 🐻‍❄️
caption: Polar bear hair is transparent and hollow; it only looks white because it scatters light. Underneath is black skin and up to about 4 inches of fat.
